summary: Spike the wasm-emit JIT / AOT-to-wasm path: generate a wasm module for a hot kernel at runtime, instantiate it in V8 (node+deno), and measure instantiate/codegen overhead, steady-state speedup vs the interpreter, and the crossover point — to decide if wasm-emit JIT is worth building for hot Luau kernels in the browser. Then adversarially verify.

build.summary: Built the wasm-emit JIT / AOT-to-wasm path end-to-end for the grabby IAUS argmax kernel (6 actions x 4 considerations, *1.25 momentum, data-dependent inputs via a per-iteration LCG so nothing constant-folds) and measured it 4 ways in wasm-in-V8 (node v25 + deno 2.8, both V8 14.9): (1) a REAL big-match register interpreter — the actual spike-sk-rustia skeleton VM, path-depended — executing the kernel bytecode; (2) the same kernel as a plain Rust fn compiled to wasm32 (the steady-state ceiling); (3) a wasm module GENERATED AT RUNTIME with the wasm-encoder crate, compiled+instantiated in V8 and run; (4) a shared-heap variant whose generated module IMPORTS the host linear memory and routes the inputs array through that heap. All six paths produce a BIT-IDENTICAL FNV checksum (0xd385c5e57bdc3538 for seed 0x12345678) that also matches the native build, and the checksum changes per-seed (data-dependent, not folded). Results: interpreter ~803 ns/op, static-AOT ~3.38 ns/op (237x), runtime-gen naive ~10.0 ns/op (80x), runtime-gen unrolled/kind-specialized ~4.57 ns/op (176x; within 1.35x of LLVM AOT), shared-heap ~4.58 ns/op (no measurable bounds-check penalty). Fixed cost (codegen ~2.5-3.3us + sync compile ~0.65us + sync instantiate ~1.1us) ~= 4.7us. CROSSOVER = ~6 kernel-ops. Verdict: GO for grabby (called tens of millions of times -> ~176x net win, fixed cost amortized after 6 calls); CONDITIONAL for general short-lived scripts (gate JIT on call_count x interp_cost > ~5us standup).
build.what_built:
KERNEL: grabby IAUS f64 argmax. Given arr[0..4] in [0,1) and last action index in 0..6, for each of 6 actions compute prod of 4 curves (kind=(a+c)%3: 0=>x*x, 1=>x, 2=>1-x), apply *1.25 if a==last, argmax (strict <, first-wins). Inputs produced per-iteration by an LCG (state=state*6364136223846793005+1442695040888963407; x=(state>>11)*2^-53; last=(state>>32)%6) so the loop cannot be hoisted/constant-folded. Every path folds (best, best_v.bits) into an FNV checksum -> identical across paths == "same kernel logic" proof + anti-DCE.

INTERPRETER PATH (1): path-depends on the ACTUAL measured skeleton crate /workspace/src/rustia/spikes/spike-sk-rustia and calls its Vm::run (NaN-boxed Value, fixed-width Instr, one big match->br_table dispatch) on build_argmax_f64() bytecode, FUEL=false (interpreter's best case, conservative for the JIT argument). Compiled to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Not the kernel inlined — a real bytecode VM.

STATIC-AOT PATH (2): kernel_aot() — the identical kernel as a plain Rust fn, compiled to wasm32 by rustc/LLVM (opt-level 3, lto). The "ideal compiled code the engine JITs" ceiling.

RUNTIME-GENERATED PATH (3): emit_module_cfg() in src/lib.rs uses the wasm-encoder crate to BUILD a wasm binary at runtime that contains the identical driver loop + LCG input-gen + argmax kernel + checksum fold, exporting run_gen(iters,seed)->i64. Two emitters: gen_loop (action loop kept, curve-kind chosen via branchless wasm `select`) and gen_opt (both loops unrolled so kind=(a+c)%3 is a codegen-time constant and only the chosen curve is emitted — AOT-to-wasm specialization). codegen runs INSIDE the host wasm module (exported codegen_run/codegen_run_opt), i.e. codegen itself is timed in wasm-in-V8 (the in-browser scenario); it returns (ptr<<32|len) into the host's own linear memory, the JS harness reads the bytes out, then does new WebAssembly.Module(bytes)+new Instance (sync) and await WebAssembly.instantiate (async) with real timing, then runs it. Proven generated-at-runtime: bytes live above __heap_base in the host heap, start with magic 00 61 73 6d v1, WebAssembly.validate=true.

SHARED-HEAP VARIANT (4): emit_module_cfg(shared=true,...) emits a module with an (import "env" "memory") and, each iteration, f64.store's the 4 generated inputs into the host heap at base+{0,8,16,24} then f64.load's them straight back (bounds-checked round-trip through the VM heap) before the kernel. Instantiated with {env:{memory: host.exports.memory}}; base = host scratch_ptr() (a [f64;16] static in the host heap). run_shared(iters,seed,base).

HARNESS: harness.mjs runs in node v25 and deno (both V8). best-of-9 over ITERS=2,000,000 with 5 warmup calls (TurboFan tier-up); fixed costs are means over 4000 reps (plus best-of-500). src/main.rs is a native sanity bin that confirms interp==aot natively and writes the 4 generated .wasm files to disk.

build.crossover_analysis:
STEADY-STATE SPEEDUP: interpreter 802.7 ns/op vs static-AOT 3.38 ns/op = 237x (the ceiling). The shippable runtime-generated (unrolled, kind-specialized) path is 4.57 ns/op = 176x over the interpreter and only 1.35x off the LLVM-AOT ceiling — i.e. runtime-emitted wasm, once V8 TurboFan-compiles it, reaches essentially compiled native speed. The naive looped emit is 10.05 ns/op = 80x. The 1.35x residual to ideal AOT is the only place gen != aot, and it is attributable to my emitter being scalar (LLVM autovectorizes/regallocs better); a production emitter could close it, but at 176x it is irrelevant to the decision.

TOTAL FIXED COST (one-time per JIT'd function): codegen ~2.95us + sync compile ~0.66us + sync instantiate ~1.08us ~= 4.68us for the unrolled path (4.15us looped, 5.2us shared). Async WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes) is ~10us (worse, scheduling overhead) — for these <1.1KB modules synchronous compile is the right standup path.

CROSSOVER = fixed_cost / per-op-saving. per-op saving = interp - gen = 802.7 - 4.57 = 798.2 ns. crossover = 4680 ns / 798.2 ns = 5.9 -> 6 kernel-ops. (looped: 4147/792.7=5.2->6; shared: 5201/798.2=6.5->7. deno reproduces 5-7.) So after just ~6 invocations the AOT-to-wasm path has paid back its entire codegen+compile+instantiate cost and every subsequent call is pure ~176x profit.

GRABBY (the question that matters): a hot per-agent decision is called MILLIONS of times (e.g. 4000 agents x thousands of ticks = 1e7-1e8 decisions per run). Crossover at 6 means standup is amortized after the first ~microsecond of simulation. Net: for 1e7 decisions, interpreter ~= 8.0 s vs AOT-to-wasm ~= 0.046 s + ~5us standup -> ~174x wall-clock reduction on the selector. Unconditional win.

GENERAL SCRIPTS: the crossover is shockingly low (6) ONLY because this kernel is compute-heavy (~800 ns interpreted). Crossover scales as ~5us / (interp_ns - 5ns). For a trivial function (interp ~20 ns) crossover ~= 5000/15 ~= 330 calls; for a function run once or twice it NEVER pays off, and JIT-ing thousands of cold one-shot functions costs more than it saves. So general scripts are CONDITIONAL: gate JIT emission on (observed call_count x per-call interpreter cost) exceeding the ~5us standup — a trivial hotness counter.
build.verdict: GO for grabby; CONDITIONAL for general scripts. CROSSOVER ~= 6 kernel-ops (node: unrolled 6 / looped 6 / shared 7; deno reproduces 5-7). A wasm-emit JIT/AOT IS worth building for hot Luau numeric kernels in the browser: a kernel emitted to wasm at runtime, instantiated in V8 (~4.7us total standup: ~3us codegen via wasm-encoder + ~0.7us sync compile + ~1.1us sync instantiate), runs at 4.57 ns/op — 176x faster than the real register interpreter (802.7 ns/op) and within 1.35x of the LLVM static-AOT ceiling (3.38 ns/op). Because the fixed cost amortizes after just ~6 calls, any function called more than a handful of times nets ahead. For grabby's per-agent decision (called 1e7-1e8 times/run) this is an unconditional ~176x win on the selector with the standup cost vanishing into the noise. For general/short-lived scripts it is CONDITIONAL: the 6-op crossover only holds for compute-heavy kernels; trivial or run-once functions may never repay the ~5us standup, so gate JIT emission behind a hotness counter (emit when observed call_count x per-call interp cost > ~5us). The shared-heap (imported host memory) variant shows JIT'd code can touch the VM heap with NO measurable bounds-check penalty (4.58 vs 4.57 ns/op).
caveats: The 802.7 ns/op interpreter is the REAL spike-sk-rustia VM but run with FUEL OFF (best-case interpreter). With the deterministic fuel meter on it is slower, so the JIT win and crossover are if anything understated — this choice is conservative for the GO verdict.

runtime-gen(unrolled) is 4.57 ns vs static-AOT 3.38 ns = 1.35x gap; runtime-gen is NOT bit-for-bit as fast as LLVM AOT. Residual is my scalar hand-emitter vs LLVM autovectorization/register allocation. A production emitter could narrow it (e.g. SIMD), but at 176x over the interpreter it does not affect the decision.

All ns/op include the per-iteration LCG input-gen (~few ns), identical across paths. It cancels in the per-op SAVING (so crossover is unaffected) and only inflates the absolute AOT/gen ns/op slightly (conservative for the speedup ratio).

Crossover counts ONLY codegen+compile+instantiate. It excludes the engineering cost of building the Luau->wasm compiler, and the runtime cost of hotness detection, type guards, and deopt/bailout. This kernel is monomorphic f64; real Luau is dynamically typed, so a real JIT needs guard+fallback paths that add per-op overhead not modeled here.
Speedups are representative of NUMERIC hot loops (exactly grabby's IAUS argmax). Polymorphic / table-heavy / string-heavy Luau will not reach 3-5 ns/op and the crossover rises accordingly.

Synchronous new WebAssembly.Module is ideal here because modules are <1.1 KB; browsers discourage large synchronous main-thread compiles. Async WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes) measured ~10us (2x the sync standup) due to promise scheduling. For big emitted modules, compile off the main thread.

Measured on Apple M-series under node v25 / deno 2.8 (both V8 14.9). JSC (Safari) and SpiderMonkey (Firefox) will differ in absolute numbers, but the structural result (emitted wasm -> ~native after a ~microsecond standup) is engine-independent.

The shared-heap variant round-trips inputs through the host heap once per iteration (store+reload, bounds-checked) and showed no penalty; a kernel doing heavy random-access heap traffic could surface a small bounds-check cost not captured by this access pattern.

verify.honesty_check: REAL interpreter: run_interp_impl (lib.rs:117) runs build_argmax_f64() bytecode through spike_sk_rustia::Vm::run::<false> (spike-sk-rustia/src/lib.rs:416-554) — a genuine register VM with one big `match i.op` dispatch over fixed-width 8-byte Instr and NaN-boxed Value, NOT the kernel inlined as Rust. The bytecode (lib.rs:276-336) realizes the identical kernel as kernel_aot (6 actions x 4 considerations, kind=(a+c)%3 -> {x*x, x, 1-x}, *1.25 if a==last, argmax strict< first-wins). REAL runtime wasm generation: harness.mjs calls host exports codegen_run/codegen_run_opt/codegen_shared(_opt) which run emit_module_cfg (lib.rs:362, wasm-encoder crate) INSIDE the host wasm module, returns (ptr<<32|len) into HX.memory.buffer; harness reads bytes out (readGen), then `new WebAssembly.Module(bytes)` + `new WebAssembly.Instance(mod,imports)` + runs inst.exports[run_gen/run_shared]. emit_module_cfg rebuilds the module from scratch on every call (Module::new + all sections) so codegen cost is genuinely re-incurred each microK iteration. NOT loading a prebuilt .wasm: the only readFileSync in harness.mjs is HOST_WASM (line 31); the on-disk gen_*.wasm files are written solely by main.rs (gencheck bin) for inspection and are never read by the harness. Instantiate timing is real: new WebAssembly.Instance(mod,imports) called in a 4000-rep microK loop (mean) + 500-rep best; async paths via WebAssembly.instantiate. Same kernel + data-dependent across all paths PROVEN by bit-identical FNV checksum 0xd385c5e57bdc3538 across interp/aot/gen_loop/gen_opt/shared_loop/shared_opt AND native (V8 prints BigInt-signed 0x-2c7a3a1a8423cac8; I verified (-0x2c7a3a1a8423cac8)&0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF == 0xd385c5e57bdc3538). Anti-DCE/anti-fold: inputs from per-iteration LCG keyed on runtime seed param (gen_inputs lib.rs:48 and emit_input/emit_last in generated wasm use identical LCG_A/LCG_C/INV_2P53 constants); checksum returned from each fn and stored/printed; black_box wraps native run inputs+outputs (main.rs:26-29). gen_proof confirms generated bytes live above __heap_base, magic 00 61 73 6d, version 1, WebAssembly.validate=true. Inspected: spike-wasmjit/src/lib.rs, src/main.rs, harness.mjs, Cargo.toml, and spike-sk-rustia/src/lib.rs.

verify.crossover_check: Re-derived from my reproduced node numbers. per-op saving (unrolled) = interp - gen_opt = 805.7 - 4.56 = 801.1 ns; fixed cost = 4.72us; crossover = 4720/801.1 = 5.9 -> 6 ops. Looped: 805.7 - 10.14 = 795.6 ns saving, fixed 4.22us -> 4216/795.6 = 5.3 -> 6. Shared unrolled: saving ~801 ns, fixed 5.44us -> 6.8 -> 7. Deno reproduced 6/6/7 too (gen_opt slower at 5.24 but saving still ~797, fixed ~4.7 -> still ~6). The ~6-kernel-op crossover and the GO verdict hold. Note crossover is intrinsically driven by the ~800ns interpreted cost of this compute-heavy kernel; it counts only codegen+compile+instantiate and excludes compiler-engineering, hotness detection, and (for real dynamically-typed Luau) guard/deopt overhead — correctly flagged in the spike's own caveats.
discrepancies: deno gen_opt reproduced at 5.24 ns/op vs claimed 4.56 (and shared_opt 5.23 vs 4.58); deno aot 3.64 vs 3.37. Higher under my run, likely background load on the M-series box. Does not change the verdict: deno crossover still 6/6/7, speedup still >150x. Node numbers reproduced essentially exactly.

Interpreter is measured with FUEL=false (fuel meter off) = interpreter best case. This is conservative for the JIT-wins argument (real fueled interp is slower, so the win/crossover is understated), and is explicitly disclosed in the spike caveats — not a cheat.

runtime-gen is 1.34-1.35x slower than LLVM static-AOT (scalar hand-emit vs LLVM autovectorization/regalloc); the spike correctly states gen != aot bit-for-bit and that it is irrelevant at 176x. Honest, not a discrepancy in claims.

Cosmetic: the 4 on-disk gen_*.wasm files could mislead a reader into thinking the harness loads them; it does not (harness only reads HOST_WASM and regenerates bytes in-VM). The .wasm files are inspection artifacts from the gencheck bin.
verify.overall: GO verdict is sound and reproduces. The spike honestly demonstrates that a Luau numeric hot kernel emitted to wasm at runtime (via wasm-encoder, codegen timed inside wasm-in-V8) and instantiated synchronously in V8 reaches ~4.57 ns/op — 176x faster than the real register-VM interpreter (805 ns/op) and within 1.35x of the LLVM static-AOT ceiling (3.38 ns/op) — for a one-time standup of ~4.7us (codegen ~3 + sync compile ~0.7 + sync instantiate ~1.05). Crossover is ~6 kernel-ops, confirmed by my re-derivation on both node and deno. Bit-identical FNV checksum across all 6 paths + native, data-dependent per-seed, is solid proof of same-kernel + anti-DCE. Single most important takeaway for the design: for grabby's per-agent decision (called 1e7-1e8x/run) the ~4.7us standup vanishes after ~6 calls and the wasm-emit JIT is an unconditional ~176x win on the selector; the ONLY load-bearing caveat for the broader Luau target is that this kernel is monomorphic f64 compute — real dynamically-typed Luau needs type guards + deopt/fallback paths whose per-op cost is NOT modeled here, so gate emission behind a hotness counter (call_count x interp_cost > ~5us) and expect the crossover/speedup to degrade for polymorphic/table/string-heavy code.
